One small change to the actor update makes RL work for flow policies on real robots, VLAs, and even image models. Here's QF3 from UC Berkeley and Amazon FAR, explained in 4 minutes!!!

A lot of robots today run on flow policies. A flow policy turns random noise into an action by following a learned velocity field, one small step at a time. Think of it as diffusion for actions. You normally train one by imitation, on a dataset of demonstrations.

Reinforcement learning is harder, because there's no dataset. The robot only has its own attempts in a replay buffer. You train a critic, Q, to score actions. The most direct way to improve the policy is then to follow the critic's gradient: predict where the flow lands in one step, and push it uphill on Q.

The catch is that if that prediction lands far from anything in the buffer, the critic is guessing. When it overestimates, the policy chases a fake peak and training falls apart which is not at all what we want!

QF3's fix is to clip the policy's velocity so its prediction stays close to the replay action, where the critic can be trusted. Past the clip, the gradient is simply masked out. It's one actor update, with a standard critic and no extra networks.

The results are pretty promising 
• Fine-tuning a pretrained bimanual VLA (ABC-VLA) with only LoRA adapters on its flow action head, VLM frozen. In the side-by-side episodes, the QF3 policy finishes bottles-in-bin 1.8× faster and plates-in-dish-rack 2.1× faster than the base policy. 
• Full fine-tuning on the robomimic Square, Tool Hang and Transport tasks. 
• Humanoids trained from scratch: they dropped QF3 into FastTD3 unchanged and deployed on real hardware for velocity tracking and motion tracking. Yes, it dances. On motion tracking it reached the same performance about 10× faster in wall-clock time than FPO++, on a single GPU. 
• The same update fine-tunes Stable Diffusion 3.5 Medium. Each prompt is a one-step episode, and the PickScore reward model plays the critic.

I like this because it's the most direct way to use a critic, made safe with a one-line idea: only trust the gradient where the critic has seen data. Teleoperated demonstrations are slow and expensive, and a policy that RL can make faster and better after imitation is a big deal.

Day 7 of teaching you how to create with AI.

The secret to cinematic AI videos isn't just the prompt. It's what happens BEFORE you generate your first shot. 🎬👀

Someone asked me yesterday how to create a good storyboard, so let's talk about it!

Whether you're creating a fashion film, product advert, UGC video, or AI movie, here's your simple roadmap. 👇

1️⃣ Start with the idea. Know what you want to create and the story you want to tell.

2️⃣ Structure your story. Give it a beginning, middle, and ending.

3️⃣ Break it into shots. Decide what happens in every scene and what your audience should see.

4️⃣ Direct the camera. Choose your angles, close-ups, camera movements, and transitions.

5️⃣ Upload your references to ChatGPT. Include your model, character, or product images and ask it to create a shot-by-shot storyboard.

6️⃣ Review before generating. Check the flow, character consistency, outfit details, and camera directions.

7️⃣ Bring it to life. Use your storyboard in Google Flow, generate your shots, and edit them together in CapCut.

Remember, a storyboard isn't just a collection of beautiful images. It's your visual roadmap!

Plan the story before you generate the scenes. That's how you gain more control over your AI videos. 🔥

💬 What's your biggest challenge: prompts, camera angles, character consistency, or video generation?

Tell me in the comments. Let's learn together! ❤️

We’re sharing more of our research, starting with our paper on outcome-routed post-training for diffusion language models.

Many standard RL methods are difficult to apply reliably to diffusion language models. Our approach avoids policy likelihood ratios and combines reward-based learning with teacher guidance.

Tool-calling accuracy (BFCL) rose from 53.55% to 88.6%, without increasing the model’s size.

The result: a more effective way to post train diffusion language models for new capabilities.

Our team will present the work at the NeurIPS 2026 DiffuLM. https://t.co/zTjk2to0hm
